source: Ash and Hu (2026) WIP: Chat-Debugging: Large Language Model as a Hardware Debugging Assistant
finding: Key work for this subfield. A case study of one fourth-year EE student using GPT-4o to debug circuits and code. Benefits found: accurate hardware facts, handles terse natural-language prompts, higher self-reported debugging confidence. Challenges: hardware debugging needs many prompts and constant human feedback.
numbers: N=1 student (alias Daniel); 3 chat logs: 11 prompts/30 min (software), 10 prompts/1 h (Pi Pico + multiplexer, ended unresolved), 7 prompts/30 min (LED circuit). Two researchers coded logs and interview. Confidence is self-reported. IRB-25-95.
quote: it does start to forget things or modify things that you had already told it.
limits: N=1, self-report, no control arm, no measured time or success. The paper does not measure overconfidence; the 'overconfidence matches G10' link in SUBFIELDS.md is not supported by this paper directly. The student's boosted confidence is itself a possible miscalibration risk.
agent_relevance: Human-in-loop pattern: LLM proposes several root causes and test plans, human runs them and reports results (hypothesis, test, update loop). Context drift in long chats supports fresh context per attempt (S3) and restating a fixed system description each turn.

source: Ash and Hu (2026) Chat-Debugging: proposed protocol
finding: Proposes an LLM-assisted debugging protocol that follows Katz and Anderson (1987): understand system (LLM summarises datasheets), test (LLM drafts test plans), locate bug (LLM lists candidate root causes from test results), fix, then verify with LLM-drafted function tests. Human must validate every claim and correct misunderstandings.
numbers: No quantitative results. Follow-up planned: multiple students, circuits with seeded bugs, final circuit performance and time spent.
limits: Protocol is proposed from one case, untested. Authors state the LLM outputs cannot be trusted without real-world analysis.
agent_relevance: Maps onto schema states: frame, hypothesis generation, test design, evidence update. The rule that results come from the bench, not the LLM, is G10 in practice.

source: Ash and Hu (2026) Chat-Debugging: observed failures of context handling
finding: In the LED conversation, asked 'can i use gp15 instead', GPT-4o answered that GPIO 15 is not a power input, misreading the question; the user had to clarify 'i mean gp15 for the led'. Giving a whole multi-board setup at once made the model put several parts on the same pins, so the user fed context in small pieces.
numbers: Anecdotes from conversation 3 (7 prompts) and the interview. In conversation 2 the model ordered root causes by its own guess of test difficulty or time; the hardware fixes became too complex and the session ended unresolved.
limits: Single user, single model (GPT-4o), qualitative.
agent_relevance: Supports incremental context and restating constraints (pin map, voltages) in a structured state block; ordering hypotheses by cheap test first works but can strand the search on costly ones.

source: Cui et al. (2026) HWE-Bench: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Real-World Hardware Bug Repair Tasks
finding: 417 real bug-fix tasks from 6 open-source hardware repos, agents run in containers. Best agent resolves about 71%. Hard repos (OpenTitan, XiangShan) lose 20 to 30 points. Verilog vs Chisel matters little compared with project-level factors.
numbers: GPT-5.4 xhigh (Codex CLI) 295/417 = 70.7%; Claude Opus 4.6 (Claude Code) 284 = 68.1%; Sonnet 4.6 278 = 66.7%; GLM 5.1 263 = 63.1%; Qwen3.6 Plus 52.5%; DeepSeek V3.2 52.0%; Kimi K2.5 47.7%. 45/417 (10.8%) unsolved by all 7. Budget 6 h and 500 iterations per task. OpenTitan 245 tasks, Ibex 35, CVA6 35, Caliptra 16, XiangShan 54, Rocket Chip 32.
quote: the choice of HDL has limited impact relative to the project-level factors discussed above.
limits: Simulation-based (Verilator-only subset is 172 tasks); real PR fixes; bug-category counts only in a figure.
agent_relevance: Realistic ceiling for agentic hardware bug repair with tools is about 70% on tasks with test oracles. Difficulty is set by repository complexity, so spend by difficulty (G12).

source: Cui et al. (2026) HWE-Bench: failure analysis and cost
finding: Three failure modes: localization (agents edit the file where the failure shows, not the file that owns the bug), hardware-semantic reasoning (patch compiles but breaks the hardware contract, e.g. incomplete state transitions or partial handshakes), and cross-artifact coordination (RTL fixed but configs or generated mirrors not). Claude models mostly used static analysis and rarely built or simulated; GPT-5.4 explored most but had lowest patch precision.
numbers: File-level precision: GPT-5.4 0.619, Opus 4.6 0.928, Sonnet 4.6 0.916, GLM 5.1 0.892, Qwen 0.878, DeepSeek 0.865, Kimi 0.859. Mean tool calls per task: GPT-5.4 77.7, Opus 20.0, Sonnet 18.6. Mean cost: GPT-5.4 $1.81, Opus $0.51, Sonnet $0.26, DeepSeek $0.10.
limits: Explanations of model style are the authors' reading of traces.
agent_relevance: Symptom location is not cause location: add an explicit step to trace the signal back to its owner before editing. More tool calls bought a few points of recall but not precision.

source: ChipBench (2026) A Next-Step Benchmark for Evaluating LLM Performance in AI-Aided Chip Design
finding: Debugging suite of 89 injected-bug cases (arithmetic 24, assignment 30, timing 29, state machine 6). Pass rates are low and spread widely across models; the best pass@1 model is not the best pass@10 model. One-shot example helped 8 models and hurt 13.
quote: LLMs generally demonstrate 5%-20% higher pass rates on debugging than code generation.
limits: Author-reported. The very low Sonnet and Gemini 2.5 Pro scores look like protocol or format failures (my inference, not stated). Per-model one-shot numbers only in a figure.
agent_relevance: Gain of about 20 to 25 points from pass@1 to pass@10 shows many draws plus an external checker beat one answer (G12, many-draws note). One-shot examples are not safe by default.

source: ARSP (2025) Automated Repair of Verilog Designs via Semantic Partitioning
finding: Splitting a buggy module into semantic fragments and repairing each with a tuned small model (DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B LoRA) beats prompting large models on the whole module. Partitioning alone adds 11.6 points pass@1. But frontier models got worse when given fragments.
numbers: 132 cases from 33 designs, 1-4 injected bugs, avg 219 lines. pass@1/pass@5 (%): ARSP 77.92/83.88; Claude-3.7 40.15/52.42; MEIC 35.00/37.56; DeepSeek-V3 28.71/48.16; Strider 28.03; VeriDebug 4.73/5.41. Ablation: base 4.09, seed data 60.6, plus synthetic 66.32, plus partition 77.92. Partition LLM success 96.51% (99.24% with rules). Manual study: 142 of 145 bugs lie in one fragment.
limits: Injected not real bugs; small test set; fragment-level prompting hurt Claude-3.7 (32.16 vs 40.15) and DeepSeek-V3 (22.95 vs 28.71), blamed on distribution shift; VeriDebug low score blamed on its training data.
agent_relevance: Locality: most bugs sit in one small region, so localise then repair works. Decomposition is not free for strong generic models; test it per model before adding.

source: Caminha et al. (2025) Evaluating LLMs and Prompting Strategies for Automated Hardware Diagnosis from Textual User-Reports
finding: Classifying 853 user reports (FACTO dataset) into 8 faulty-component classes. Most models land at F1 about 0.70 to 0.77 whatever the prompt; chain-of-thought gains are small and uneven. Scaling flattens near 30B parameters.
limits: Text only, 8 coarse classes, class imbalance; no instrument readings. Tiny models failed on output format, not diagnosis. Prompt effects mostly inside error bars except for small models.
agent_relevance: For coarse triage from symptom text, prompt wording barely matters; do not expect scaffold wins from wording alone (G11, think briefly). Format enforcement matters for small models.

source: Ahmad, Thakur, Tan, Karri, Pearce (2023) Fixing Hardware Security Bugs with Large Language Models
finding: Early study: Codex and CodeGen repair security bugs in Verilog. Success depends strongly on instruction variant, temperature and model. Lower temperature was better. Bugs needing a new always block or removal of a line were hardest.
numbers: 10 bugs (MITRE CWE, OpenTitan, Hack@DAC-21); 20 responses per bug per temperature {0.1,0.3,0.5,0.7,0.9} per instruction variant. code-davinci-002 2371/5000 = 47.4% correct repairs; davinci-001 40.4%; cushman-001 33.1%; CodeGen 6.68%. OpenAI models best at t=0.1, CodeGen at 0.3. Every bug got at least one fix; 9 of 10 bugs reached 100% with best settings. Bugs 3 and 4 over 50%; bugs 2, 6, 7, 9 under 25%.
limits: Best settings were picked per bug after seeing results (an oracle choice), so 100% overstates real use. Old models (2022). Repair judged by simulation and security tests.
agent_relevance: Per-bug tuned settings are an oracle; a real agent needs a checker in the loop, not parameter search. Descriptive signal names helped, so clean input helps (S1).

source: Hu et al. (2026) When LLMs Over-Answer: Measuring and Mitigating Quality Issues in LLM-Based HDL Question Answering
finding: Study of 6,246 Stack Overflow hardware-description-language Q&A posts (Conceptual, Debugging, Generation, Optimization) and 19 HDL engineers. LLM answers often bury the correct content under redundant alternatives and padding. A multi-agent answering framework reduced this.
numbers: 65.7% of LLM answers bury correct content under redundant alternatives; 69.1% have verbose padding; 49.0% do not fully align with expert answers; yet 58.3% of 19 engineers preferred LLM answers for readability. Multi-agent framework, 4 LLMs, 5-point judge: core-answer quality 3.71 to 4.67; non-core 3.72 to 4.23.
limits: Only an overview/abstract page seen, not the full paper. Judge is an LLM; engineers had 1-3 years of experience. Different Hu from the Ash and Hu pair.
agent_relevance: Over-answering hedges by listing many options; readers like it though it is less correct. Reader preference is a bad proxy for correctness (G5: blind, length-normalised judges). Agent should commit to ranked hypotheses with tests.

source: Wang et al. (2025) VeriDebug: A Unified LLM for Verilog Debugging via Contrastive Embedding and Guided Correction
finding: Fine-tuned model that finds and fixes Verilog bugs in one parameter space, using contrastive embeddings for localisation and guided correction.
numbers: Best variant 64.7 Acc@1 on bug fixing; abstract cites open-source state of the art at 11.3 and GPT-3.5-turbo at 36.6.
limits: Abstract only. In the later ARSP benchmark VeriDebug scored only 4.73 pass@1 (see c07), so the headline does not transfer across benchmarks.
agent_relevance: Benchmark-specific tuned numbers do not transfer; prefer held-out sets with an execution oracle.

source: MEIC (2024) LLM-assisted debugging of RTL code
finding: Iterative LLM loop for RTL syntax and functional errors that manages LLM uncertainty; reports far faster than engineers.
numbers: Syntax error fix rate 93%; function error fix rate 78%; up to 48x speedup versus experienced engineers; dataset of 178 common RTL errors.
limits: Abstract only; models and loop details not read. ARSP's own benchmark gave MEIC 35.00 pass@1 (c07), much lower.
agent_relevance: A simulator-feedback loop is the standard agent pattern here; functional bugs are fixed less often than syntax bugs.

source: Towards LLM-based Root Cause Analysis of Hardware Design Failures (2025)
finding: LLMs explain root causes of EDA-tool failures well. Retrieval-augmented generation helped weak models little or hurt, and made models ignore a no-code instruction.
numbers: 34 errors (19 synthesis, 15 runtime), 5 responses each, 170 total. Pass@5/Avg@5 runtime baseline: gpt-3.5 46.7/14.7, GPT-4o 93.3/80.0, o3-mini 100/86.7, DeepSeek R1 93.3/84.0. RAG: gpt-3.5 runtime 33.3/13.3 (worse); o3-mini synthesis 100/100. Top-6 chunks with text-embedding-3-small. Nearly 100% of RAG responses attempted a fix despite 'do not give code'.
limits: Only 34 samples, manual grading, single-turn, versions will change.
agent_relevance: Retrieval can reduce instruction compliance; check compliance after adding context. Error-log reading is nearly solved by strong models, so the hard part is physical and system-level diagnosis.

source: Saini (2026) EDA Bench: Testing Whether Language-Model Agents Build Functioning PCBs
finding: Agents that build KiCad boards almost always produce files that open, but nearly none work at the connectors. Agents stopped without running the design-rule or connectivity checks.
numbers: 35 tasks. Best archived row 1.48% under revised grader; fresh medium-reasoning sweep 2.18% (task-bootstrap 95% CI for xhigh [0.0282, 0.0662]). Audit of 99 saved projects: wrong pin mapping 76/99, isolated or split nets 73/99, shorts 70/99, missing circuits 70/99, unpowered active parts 18/99. Six retained traces built 6/6 projects, scored mean 0.04167, none ran ERC, DRC or ngspice.
limits: Design reconstruction, not diagnosis. One output per task, many harness failures (auth, empty streams), single author, no human-engineer agreement measured.
agent_relevance: Strong support for G10: parseable and plausible is not correct; require the tool check before stopping. Direct sign of premature closure by agents.

source: Qiu et al. (2026) HWE-Bench (board-level schematic design, arXiv 2603.18102)
finding: Models pass many static rule checks on generated board netlists but almost never produce a fully correct design. Failures are hallucinated connections on ambiguous pins and context overload on large pin counts.
numbers: 300 tasks, 8 domains, 2,914 datasheets. Fully correct designs: Claude Sonnet 4.5 8.15%, GPT-5.2 6.58%, others 4.4-5.16%. Static checks mean 71.84% (Claude Sonnet 4.5 77.73%, Grok-4 63.46%); SPICE mean 58.65% (Claude 67.92%). Static by domain: Industrial 83.05%, Automotive 77.03%, Aerospace 64.08%; SPICE lowest IoT 45.00%, Telecom 49.72%. Temperature 0.1, 6 models.
limits: Same name as arXiv 2604.14709 (also called HWE-Bench). Text and tables disagree on whether SPICE or static is higher (tables: static higher). Decomposition not ablated; datasheet-to-JSON extraction accuracy not reported. No overconfidence measure.
agent_relevance: Gap between pass-on-checks (about 72%) and fully correct (about 8%) means partial verification overstates correctness. Models invent connections on ambiguous pins, so require datasheet grounding with quoted pin tables.

source: UniPCB (2026) A Unified Vision-Language Benchmark for PCB inspection (arXiv 2601.19222)
finding: General multimodal LLMs hallucinate and localise PCB defects poorly. A domain-tuned 7B model with chain-of-thought training more than doubles localisation F1. In one-shot settings competitors over-predict defects.
numbers: 6,581 images, 23,359 bilingual QA pairs, 14 subtasks. Qwen2.5-VL-7B based PCB-GPT: F1 22.3 to 51.1, accuracy 48.7 to 69.5 after full pipeline. Localisation F1 reading: PCB-GPT 51.1 vs Gemini 2.5 Pro 23.6, GPT-5 20.2. Accuracy fully labelled: Gemini 2.5 Pro 76.4, GPT-5 73.1, PCB-GPT 72.5. External PCB-Bank zero-shot F1: PCB-GPT 52.1, AnomalyGPT 45.3, GPT-5 33.0.
limits: Table headers were garbled in my read, so the F1 column identification is partly inference. Visual inspection, not electrical diagnosis.
agent_relevance: Language fluency does not give spatial grounding; for visual boards use a detector or crop tool, not free-form description. Over-prediction of defects is a calibration issue.

source: Lee, Vidyaratne, Farahat, Gupta (2025) Exploring LLM-based Frameworks for Fault Diagnosis
finding: LLMs given sensor data from an HVAC simulator detect faults about as well as a simple rule baseline and do better with summary statistics than raw series. Multi-LLM systems with specialised prompts improved fault-classification sensitivity. In repeated fault cycles with feedback appended, LLMs failed to calibrate and kept predicting faults when none existed.
numbers: Anomaly detection F1 0.79-0.85, accuracy 0.66-0.73; rule baseline F1 0.85, accuracy 0.73. Best LLM config (GPT-4o, window 36) very close to the rule baseline. Fault classification F1 up to 0.59 for best configs; rule baseline accuracy 0.71 with zero precision, recall and F1 (predicts the normal class). Window 36 best; 48 worse. GPT-4.1-nano to GPT-4o gave small gains.
limits: Simulated HVAC, one prompt per setting, only GPT-4o and GPT-4.1-nano. Authors suspect the GPT-4o raw-data accuracy rise is pattern matching on history, not learning.
agent_relevance: Calibration across repeated cycles did not fix false alarms; a base-rate check outside the model is needed. Summarise raw signals before giving them to the model.

source: Lee et al. (2025) Exploring LLM-based Frameworks for Fault Diagnosis: statistical over-reliance
finding: The paper reports a tendency toward statistical over-reliance: with little system-level context the model over-generalises from statistical norms and misses valid exceptions. Reference data from normal operation did not help consistently.
numbers: No single figure; seen across anomaly-detection and classification tables. Adding normal-operation reference data had no consistent effect on F1.
limits: Based on my read of the discussion text; configuration-level counts not extracted.
agent_relevance: More context is not better by default: test whether each added block (reference data, history) helps, and drop it if not.

source: Caminha et al. (2025) Hardware diagnosis from user reports: size effect
finding: Small models can match large ones on coarse triage; gemma-2-2b nearly equals a 24B model. Pareto-frontier models: llama-3.2-1b, gemma-2-2b, mistral-small-24b.
numbers: gemma-2-2b-it best F1 0.7269 (2B) vs mistral-small-24b 0.7608 (24B). Gemma models were robust across all four prompts.
limits: Class labels coarse; an F1 ceiling near 0.76 shared by all models suggests label noise or ambiguous reports (my inference).
agent_relevance: A ceiling shared by all models points to input ambiguity, not reasoning; ask a follow-up question (a test) instead of choosing a class from a vague report.

source: Evaluating LLMs' effectiveness on real-world consumer device repair questions (2026, arXiv 2606.03331)
finding: 991-question benchmark built from real Reddit device-repair scenarios (English and Bangla); six frontier LLMs rated on correctness, completeness, practicality and safety. Models struggle with incomplete diagnostics, hardware-specific troubleshooting and high-stakes decisions.
numbers: 991 questions, 6 models, 4 metrics; accuracy numbers not on the page I read.
limits: Secondary news-site summary only; authors and numbers unchecked. Needs a read of arXiv 2606.03331.
agent_relevance: Real forum questions are under-specified; an agent should ask for missing measurements before advising a repair with damage risk.

source: Ash and Hu (2026) Chat-Debugging: background on human debugging
finding: Cites Katz and Anderson (1987) four steps and bug-location strategies (discrepancy detection, split-half, topographic, exhaustive, trial and error). Notes experts and novices alike struggle to generate multiple hypotheses. Says few works cover post-silicon or physical-circuit debugging with ML.
numbers: Electronics engineers may spend over 40% of their time troubleshooting circuits (cited from an industry web article, not a primary study).
limits: Secondary citations; the 40% figure is from an industry article.
agent_relevance: Strategy list is a ready set of operators for a diagnosis scaffold: split-half and discrepancy detection are checkable moves. See older E08 subfields for Katz and Anderson and Schaafstal.

source: Cui et al. (2026) HWE-Bench: tier contrast
finding: Easy repos: weakest model solves over half and best over 90% (Ibex, CVA6, Caliptra). Rocket Chip has over 40% configuration or integration bugs versus 20-25% elsewhere and is in the hard tier. GPT-5.4 uniquely solved 22 tasks.
numbers: GPT-5.4: CVA6 34/35 (97.1%), Ibex 32/35 (91.4%), Caliptra 15/16 (93.8%), OpenTitan 157/245 (64.1%), XiangShan 37/54 (68.5%), Rocket Chip 20/32 (62.5%). Top proprietary to top open-source gap 7.6 points.
limits: Repo difficulty is confounded with bug type and test quality.
agent_relevance: Integration-type bugs (config, interfaces) are the hard class; a fault tree should include cross-artifact check steps.

source: Cui et al. (2026) HWE-Bench: agent style differences
finding: Claude-based runs mostly read code and rarely built or simulated, yet scored within 3 points of the most exploratory agent. DeepSeek V3.2 produced the noisiest patches; Kimi K2.5 stayed too context-local.
numbers: Opus 4.6: 20.0 tool calls and 68.1% vs GPT-5.4: 77.7 tool calls and 70.7%. Cost $0.51 vs $1.81. Cache hit 99.7% vs 95.5%.
limits: Different frameworks (Claude Code vs Codex CLI) confound model and scaffold; no single-variable ablation.
agent_relevance: Scaffold and model are not separated in published scores; run our own ablation. Cheap runs near the top score argue for spending by difficulty (G12).

source: Ahmad et al. (2023) Fixing Hardware Security Bugs: instruction detail
finding: Detailed instructions raised success; the variant giving a Fix instruction in pseudo-code performed best. Bugs needing more than one line or removal of a buggy line were harder. Compared with CirFix (template-and-oracle search) using the best model at t=0.1.
numbers: 20 responses per bug and setting; max 200 repairs per heatmap cell; max 2,000 repairs per bug across models. CirFix comparison table not extracted.
limits: Instruction variants are hand-made and hard to generalise across bugs, as the authors say.
agent_relevance: A hypothesis-led instruction ('this may be a missing reset') helps more than a bare 'fix this'; a wrong hypothesis may bias the model, a risk to test.

source: Caminha et al. (2025) Hardware diagnosis from user reports: format failures
finding: Tiny models often named the right component in free text but failed to emit the required dictionary, giving F1 near 0. Few-shot examples fixed formatting.
numbers: Row values as printed in Table 2: qwen2.5-1.5b ZS 0.000, FS 0.673, CoT 0.651, CoT+FS 0.646; yi-6b ZS 0.272, CoT 0.013; deepseek-r1-distill-qwen-1.5b 0.199/0.393/0.206/0.328.
limits: Table text was flattened by PDF extraction, so column alignment for some rows is inferred.
agent_relevance: Scoring must separate format failures from diagnosis failures, else prompts look like they change ability.

source: Saini (2026) EDA Bench: grader validation and proposed stop rule
finding: Authors propose a typed connector-to-net plan, an explicit required-block checklist, and a repair loop where exact check failures are fed back before the agent may stop. These are proposals from observation, not tested ablations.
numbers: Grader responds to 271 of 295 controlled faults; 19 genuine unchanged faults. 35/35 references score 1.0 under the submitted grader; revised grader references average 0.957. Retained traces: 872 events, 226 commands, 36 file changes, 15 web operations over 6 sessions.
limits: Intervention order is observational; paired ablation only proposed. kicad-cli was missing in the agent image, partly explaining skipped checks.
agent_relevance: The proposed fix (check output feeds back, no stop until diagnostics pass) is G10 plus an S7 counterexample search; here untested on hardware.

source: Large Language Models and Attention-Based AI for Hardware Design and Security: Progress, Challenges, and Opportunities (2025)
finding: Survey listing LLM work in hardware design, bug localisation, retrieval-augmented repair and security.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Seen only in a search listing, not opened.
agent_relevance: Pointer for forward citation search if needed.
